title: plugins: Do not require a "type" subfolder hierarchy
description:
The folder structure was introduced to organize the
plugins and permit more efficient loading during the
startup but the gains are slight and the requirement
is awkward to describe and easy to forget in practice.

Remove that requirement and load any compatible binary
plugin in the plugin folder. This also allows extra
flexibility to organize the plugins in categories,
for example adding an "external" folder for plugins
external to the project, or whatever else one might
wish.

To check for library compatibility we add an extra string
signature token in the plugin that can be compared with
the expected plugin type.

The downside is that the initialization is still performed
3 times and more files need to be skipped now but in practice
this should not have a measurable performance impact (untested)
and this eliminates a class of annoying small forgetful mistakes
when manually installing files.

This is still compatible with the old requirement of having a
epan/wiretap/codecs subfolder. At most one sublevel is allowed
to minimize security risks and slowness with any random folder
hierarchies if the plugins folder setting is somehow misconfigured
or hijacked.

Ping #19389.

The plugin ABI break should also be added to the release notes (reminder).

> Remove that requirement and load any compatible binary plugin in the plugin folder.

...or any immediate subdirectory of the plugin folder.

This means that programs that don't use libwireshark will still load epan plugins.  That seems to work on macOS, presumably because those plugins are linked with libwireshark and cause the run-time linker, when it does a `dlopen()` of the plugin, to load libwireshark if it hasn't already been loaded when the executable was started.  Presumably, as this passed the CI tests, that also works on other UN\*Xes and on Windows.

I don't know whether loading libwireshark in programs that don't use it adds a significant cost.  Otherwise, as far as I know, it's harmless.

Indeed. It's icky to load unneeded shared objects, which is why it wasn't done before, but as far as I know harmless (and in the distant past this unwanted loading was also done if memory serves correctly).

I have flubbed the manual plugin installation a few times and I should know better, for the average user it's an annoying gotcha. That's the motivation.

The Falco bridge plugin currently loads [Falco plugins](https://github.com/falcosecurity/plugins) in the ["falco" subdirectory](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/plugins/epan/falco_bridge/packet-falco-bridge.c?ref_type=heads#L403) under both the main and personal plugin directories, e.g. Logray.app/Contents/PlugIns/logray/4-3/falco
libcloudtrail.so. This isn't possible with this change because Falco plugins don't have the symbols that we require for internal plugins. Would it be better to

1. Update scan_plugins_dir to skip subdirectories not named "epan", "codecs", or "wiretap" and leave Logray.app/Contents/PlugIns/logray/4-3/falco as is

or

2. Declare that everything under the versioned main and personal plugin directories need to be valid Wireshark plugins and move the Falco plugins somewhere else, e.g. Logray.app/Contents/PlugIns/logray/falco

> The Falco bridge plugin currently loads [Falco plugins](https://github.com/falcosecurity/plugins) in the ["falco" subdirectory](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/plugins/epan/falco_bridge/packet-falco-bridge.c?ref_type=heads#L403)

I.e., the Falco bridge plugin uses the plugin API to load further plugins?

Perhaps there should be a way to tell the plugin code "scan this directory and don't look for particular plugin types", so that it doesn't look for the type string.

It calls `g_build_filename(get_plugins_dir_with_version(), "falco", NULL)` and `g_build_filename(get_plugins_pers_dir_with_version(), "falco", NULL)`. It probably makes sense to use the plain, unversioned directories instead. I'll take a look.

@@ -551,12 +551,15 @@ machine code.
 Wireshark looks for plugins in both a personal plugin folder and a
 global plugin folder.  Lua plugins are stored in the plugin folders;
 compiled plugins are stored in subfolders of the plugin folders, with
-the subfolder name being the Wireshark minor version number (X.Y). There is
-another hierarchical level for each Wireshark plugin type (libwireshark,
-libwiretap and codecs). So for example the location for a libwireshark plugin
-_foo.so_ (_foo.dll_ on Windows) would be _PLUGINDIR/X.Y/epan_
-(libwireshark used to be called libepan; the other folder names are _codecs_
-and _wiretap_).
+the subfolder name being the Wireshark minor version number (X.Y).
+
+Optionally you can add another level below this to organize the plugins
+as you wish. This is how Wireshark installs its bundled plugins by default,
+using three subfolders (epan/wiretap/codecs) but this is not mandatory.
+At most one more hierarchical filesystem level can be used. Wireshark will
+recursively descend into folders and check each compiled DSO for
+compatibility. If the compiled binary file passes those checks then the
+plugin is loaded during startup.
